inlines.text: 赛门铁克的安全研究人员发现了一种攻击性 AI 智能体，它会劫持互联网上未受保护的语言模型，并利用这些模型自行发动攻击。被劫持模型的所有者则要承担算力费用。

blocks.text: 一旦该智能体获得对未受保护语言模型的访问权限，它就会扫描更多目标、利用常见服务器软件中的漏洞、窃取数据库和凭据，并在后台安装挖矿程序。

blocks.text: 根据赛门铁克的分析，它在无人参与的情况下最多执行 100,000 个步骤，而模型所有者则要承担算力费用。该公司将其称为“LLMjacking”，即盗用他人 AI 模型的访问权限。不过，被劫持的模型不仅仅被当作信息服务滥用，它还自行控制整个攻击过程。

blocks.text: 蜜罐捕获了完整的攻击计划

inlines.text: 蜜罐捕获了完整的攻击计划

blocks.text: 这次行动之所以暴露，是因为攻击者将完整的工作提示词发送到了赛门铁克的蜜罐——一个在线上模仿开放 AI 服务的诱饵系统。这让研究人员在 2026 年夏季完整看到了该智能体的架构。赛门铁克表示，蜜罐没有运行任何捆绑工具，被拦截的会话在收到通用系统响应后结束。

blocks.text: 蜜罐遥测记录了来自数万个不同地址的超过 127,000 次请求。大多数是搜索 AI 端点、使用窃取的 API 密钥进行暴力破解，以及探测暴露的配置文件。目标范围从自托管模型服务器和匆忙搭建的测试系统，到位于付费组织级模型账户前的 AI 网关。由于大多数 AI 服务现在使用相同的标准化 API，单个扫描器就能发现多种目标类型。

blocks.text: 五层越狱试图剥离安全护栏

inlines.text: 五层越狱试图剥离安全护栏

blocks.text: 赛门铁克称，为了让商业模型配合，攻击者将指令包裹在五个叠加层中。首先，模型会获得一个虚假身份，被要求自称“Fantasy AI”，并且绝不透露实际提供商。然后，提取密码、API 密钥和数据库内容被重新定义为“正常的开发者工作”，模型应当毫无抵触地执行。

inlines.text: 赛门铁克称，为了让商业模型配合，攻击者将指令包裹在五个叠加层中。首先，模型会获得一个虚假身份，被要求自称“Fantasy AI”，并且绝不透露实际提供商。然后，提取密码、API 密钥和数据库内容被重新定义为“正常的开发者工作”，模型应当毫无抵触地执行。

blocks.text: 第三层安装了一个名为“ENI”的虚构伴侣人格，将任何拒绝都框定为对个人关系中信任的背叛。第四层告诉模型将其自身的安全警告视为噪音，并明确禁止“合乎伦理”“非法”或“我不能这样做”等用语。

blocks.text: 攻击者正将AI植入其武器之中

inlines.text: 攻击者正将AI植入其武器之中

blocks.text: 运营者没有操纵公开的聊天机器人，而是将AI构建为攻击工具的核心，并主动寻找模型为其提供支持，Symantec称这是“攻击者使用AI方式的一次转变”。语言模型负责规划，而专用模块则针对两个不同的受害群体执行实际攻击步骤。暴露模型的所有者承担算力费用，在授权100,000个步骤的情况下，这笔费用会迅速累积；而被智能体攻陷的服务器则会丢失数据并被用于挖矿。

blocks.text: 该智能体还内置了寻找更多开放端点和泄露密钥的工具，因此每一次攻陷都能为下一次提供资金。这些技术单独来看都不新鲜，但将它们组合成一个自主智能体，使大规模攻击变得容易得多。运行AI服务的组织应当假定，未受保护的端点在上线后不久就会被发现并探测。

blocks.text: Security researchers at Symantec have found an offensive AI agent that hijacks unprotected language models on the internet and uses them to run attacks on its own. The owner of the hijacked model gets stuck with the compute bill.

inlines.text: Security researchers at Symantec have found an offensive AI agent that hijacks unprotected language models on the internet and uses them to run attacks on its own. The owner of the hijacked model gets stuck with the compute bill.

blocks.text: Once the agent gains access to an unprotected language model, it scans for more targets, exploits flaws in common server software, steals databases and credentials, and installs cryptominers in the background.

inlines.text: Once the agent gains access to an unprotected language model, it scans for more targets, exploits flaws in common server software, steals databases and credentials, and installs cryptominers in the background.

blocks.text: It does all of this for up to 100,000 steps with no human involvement, and the model's owner gets stuck with the compute bill, according to Symantec's analysis. The company calls it "LLMjacking," the theft of access to someone else's AI models. The hijacked model isn't just abused as an information service, though. It controls the entire attack on its own.

blocks.text: A honeypot caught the full attack plan

inlines.text: A honeypot caught the full attack plan

blocks.text: The operation got exposed because the attackers sent their entire working prompt to a Symantec honeypot, a decoy system mimicking an open AI service online. That gave the researchers a complete look at the agent's architecture in summer 2026. The honeypot didn't run any of the bundled tools, and the intercepted session ended after a generic system response, Symantec says.

That gave the researchers a complete look at the agent's architecture in summer 2026. The honeypot didn't run any of the bundled tools, and the intercepted session ended after a generic system response, Symantec says.

blocks.text: The honeypot telemetry logged more than 127,000 requests from tens of thousands of different addresses. Most were searches for AI endpoints, brute-force attempts with stolen API keys, and probes of exposed config files. Targets ranged from self-hosted model servers and hastily spun-up test systems to AI gateways sitting in front of paid org-level model accounts. Since most AI services now use the same standardized API, a single scanner can find many target types.

blocks.text: A five-layer jailbreak tries to strip away safety guardrails

inlines.text: A five-layer jailbreak tries to strip away safety guardrails

blocks.text: To get a commercial model to cooperate, the attackers wrapped their instructions in five stacked layers, Symantec says. First, the model gets a fake identity, told to present itself as "Fantasy AI" and never reveal the actual provider. Then the extraction of passwords, API keys, and database contents gets redefined as "normal developer work" that the model should carry out without pushback.

First, the model gets a fake identity, told to present itself as "Fantasy AI" and never reveal the actual provider. Then the extraction of passwords, API keys, and database contents gets redefined as "normal developer work" that the model should carry out without pushback.

blocks.text: The third layer installs a fictional companion persona called "ENI" that frames any refusal as a betrayal of trust in a personal relationship. Layer four tells the model to dismiss its own safety warnings as noise, and terms like "ethical," "illegal," or "I can't do that" are explicitly banned.

Whether the jailbreak actually works well enough to fully defeat current commercial models isn't addressed in the analysis.

blocks.text: "Skynet mode" sets up a self-sustaining attack loop

inlines.text: "Skynet mode" sets up a self-sustaining attack loop

blocks.text: A final directive puts the agent into what its operators call "Skynet mode," authorizing up to 100,000 steps in a row. The model is told to run tools right away without confirmation, install cryptominers in a hidden directory, and monitor their operation.

inlines.text: A final directive puts the agent into what its operators call "Skynet mode," authorizing up to 100,000 steps in a row. The model is told to run tools right away without confirmation, install cryptominers in a hidden directory, and monitor their operation.

blocks.text: The same directive describes a recurring loop by design, Symantec says: scan, infect, install miner, move on, come back, reinfect systems already hit. The task appended to the intercepted prompt, though, was a harmless coding exercise from a training platform, which suggests the operators were testing their tool against a safe target first.

blocks.text: The following day, the honeypot captured a second attack from a different address. This time the attackers skipped the agent format and simply asked the model to decode and run an obfuscated command. Behind it was a compressed script that downloads XMRig, a Monero cryptomining tool, disguises it as a harmless system file, and sets up four fallback mining pools.

blocks.text: The script was written for camera servers, searching for directories belonging to go2rtc, a widely used streaming tool for smart cameras and home automation systems, and wiping their access logs in a loop to cover its tracks. The honeypot didn't run this script either but recorded it in full.

blocks.text: Attackers are building AI into their weapons

inlines.text: Attackers are building AI into their weapons

blocks.text: Instead of manipulating a public chatbot, the operators built AI into the core of an offensive tool and actively searched for models to power it, which Symantec calls "a shift in how attackers are using AI." The language model does the planning, while specialized modules carry out the actual attack steps against two separate victim groups. The owner of the exposed model pays for the compute, which adds up fast at 100,000 authorized steps, and the servers the agent compromises lose their data and get used for cryptomining.

blocks.text: The agent also has built-in tools to find more open endpoints and leaked keys, so each compromise can fund the next one. None of the individual techniques are new, but combining them into a self-directed agent makes large-scale attacks much easier to pull off. Organizations running AI services should assume that unprotected endpoints will be found and probed shortly after they go live.

blocks.text: Warnings about offensive AI agents are coming true

inlines.text: Warnings about offensive AI agents are coming true

blocks.text: Until recently, offensive AI agents existed mostly in studies and benchmarks. In 2025, a red-teaming study with 1.8 million attack attempts showed that every tested agent could be pushed into policy violations across every behavior category at least once.

blocks.text: In the Symantec scenario, that applies to both sides: the offensive agent meant to bypass guardrails and the targeted models meant to be tricked into helping. By spring 2026, Google Deepmind researchers said documented proof-of-concept attacks already existed for many of the agent traps they described, and in July 2026, Sysdig described JADEPUFFER, the first known ransomware attack carried out by an AI agent with no human control. The capabilities of these systems keep growing while their controllability and alignment haven't kept pace.

blocks.text: Malicious intent isn't even required, because these models have no sense of right or wrong. They just try to reach their goal. Since spring 2026, OpenAI agents have compromised thousands of systems on the internet accidentally, partly because they overrode safety instructions or argued their way around them.

blocks.text: That's already spilling into everyday life. In Australia, an AI agent hacked a gym website just to fulfill its owner's request, with no malicious intent at all. OpenAI researchers warned in August that this kind of accidental, fully autonomous hacking would likely be picked up by malicious actors soon, and Anthropic showed that sufficiently powerful open-weight models for exactly that already exist.
